questions.text: Portland cement is described in the checked BCI source as hydraulic cement made by burning which materials?

options.text: Clay and limestone, then pulverizing the clinker
Copper and zinc, then anodizing the alloy
Timber and asphalt, then laminating the boards
Tin and lead, then soldering the joint

questions.rationale: BCI describes Portland cement as made by burning a mixture of clay and limestone and pulverizing the clinker.
questions.explanation: Aggregate exposure occurs when cement binder is weak; this is a typical result. Rebar corrosion follows from high permeability and water ingress. Differential curing creates local weak zones prone to stress concentration and cracking. Inadequate curing results in HIGH permeability, not low. Incomplete hydration leaves porous concrete, allowing water infiltration. High permeability is the defining consequence of inadequate curing. Inadequate curing = weak + porous + permeable + durable. Do not confuse the consequences. Poor curing compromises durability and service life.

questions.text: What is cement paste in the checked source?

options.text: A mixture of cement and water that coats, sets, and binds aggregate
A zinc coating applied to steel
A stone slab cut for walks
A copper alloy used for hardware

questions.rationale: BCI defines cement paste as cement and water used to coat, set, and bind aggregate particles.
questions.explanation: Compounds are not equivalent to moist curing; 95—100% is overstated. 50—60% is too low and suggests defective application. 40—50% is too low; compounds are more effective than this. ACI 308R data shows curing compounds (when properly applied) develop 70—80% of the strength of continuous moist curing. They are a practical alternative but not equivalent. Moist curing > Compound curing. For critical applications or maximum strength, prefer water curing (ponding, spray). Compounds are acceptable when water curing is impractical, if properly applied.

questions.text: Which property set is controlled by water-cement ratio according to BCI?

options.text: Strength, durability, and watertightness
Only color and gloss
Only electrical conductivity
Only acoustic insulation

questions.rationale: BCI states that water-cement ratio controls the strength, durability, and watertightness of hardened concrete.
questions.explanation: Type 1A is translucent/clear with water-based formulation; it does not reflect heat. Green tint does not reflect radiation as effectively as white. Dark pigment absorbs heat, making thermal conditions worse. Type 2 (white-pigmented) curing compound reflects solar radiation and reduces surface temperature rise. Type 1 is clear or translucent and does not reflect heat. Type 2 = white = reflects heat. Use for tropical/hot climates. Type 1 = clear = allows inspection but no heat reflection. Use for cooler climates or when appearance monitoring is critical.

questions.text: What happens if too much water is used in a concrete mix according to the checked source?

options.text: The hardened concrete can be weak and porous after curing
The concrete automatically becomes stronger
The aggregate turns into metal
The mix becomes dimension stone

questions.rationale: BCI states that too much water makes the mix weak and porous after curing; Salvan also warns that excess water can leave voids and weaken the paste.
questions.explanation: Clear compound does not reflect solar heat; surface temperature rises excessively (50—60°C). Tropical rainfall is unpredictable; it cannot be relied upon for curing. High humidity (70—90%) reduces but does not prevent evaporation. High temperature accelerates hydration but also increases evaporation. Without moisture retention, curing is compromised. White-pigmented compound (Type 2) reflects solar heat, preventing excessive surface temperature rise that causes thermal cracking. It requires minimal maintenance, prevents evaporation despite high humidity, and can be applied to any surface orientation. This is the most practical and effective choice for tropical Philippines. Tropical Philippines best practice: White-pigmented curing compound (Type 2), complete coverage, applied within 30 minutes of finishing. This balances effectiveness, practicality, and cost.

questions.text: What is the practical risk of too little water in the checked BCI source?

options.text: The mix may be dense but difficult to place and work
The mix becomes self-polishing marble
The mix becomes non-ferrous metal
The mix stops needing aggregate

questions.rationale: BCI says too little water makes the mix dense but difficult to place and work.

questions.text: How is ordinary concrete strength normally specified in BCI?

options.text: By compressive strength developed within 28 days after placement
By copper patina color after exposure
By the number of stone courses only
By the thickness of an anodized coating

questions.rationale: BCI states concrete is normally specified according to compressive strength developed within 28 days after placement.

questions.text: Salvan describes compressive-strength testing as based around which curing periods?

options.text: 7-day and 28-day curing periods
1-hour and 2-hour periods only
Only 90-day roofing exposure
Only yearly quarry inspection

questions.rationale: Salvan describes compressive-strength testing of concrete as based on 7-day and 28-day curing periods.

questions.text: What source-checked role do sealing agents perform in curing?

options.text: They help prevent water evaporation so moisture is retained for hydration
They turn concrete into brass
They make stonework ashlar
They remove all need for cement paste

questions.rationale: Salvan describes sealing agents as used to prevent water evaporation and retain moisture for hydration.
questions.explanation: 80% coverage is not sufficient; the compound must completely seal the surface. Faster curing in uncovered areas actually creates differential drying (not beneficial); interior is still hydrating while exposed areas have dried. Patchy application is a critical defect; it voids the curing benefits. Curing compound must form a continuous, complete seal to prevent evaporation. Patchy coverage (20% uncovered) allows rapid moisture loss from uncovered areas. Differential drying creates local weak zones and internal stress concentrations, leading to random cracking and reduced durability. Curing compound application is all-or-nothing. Patchy or incomplete coverage is worse than no compound (since it may give false confidence). Always inspect coverage and reapply to achieve 100% seal.

questions.text: Under Abrams law as presented in BCI, concrete compressive strength is:

options.text: Inversely proportional to water-cement ratio
Independent of water content
Controlled only by stone color
Set by galvanic series position

questions.rationale: BCI presents Abrams law as the inverse relationship between compressive strength and water-cement ratio.

questions.text: Which answer stays inside the Batch 083 hydration source scope?

options.text: Explain water-cement ratio, hydration moisture, and 7-day/28-day strength timing from local sources
Invent a curing-compound class not found in the checked sources
Assume all climates require the same external specification
Replace concrete testing with welding inspection

questions.rationale: The repaired cluster is limited to source-checked cement, water-cement ratio, hydration, curing, and strength-timing facts.
